title: Kenya DPA defines 'consent' as express, unequivocal, free, specific and informed
claim: The Kenya Data Protection Act, 2019 defines consent as any manifestation of express, unequivocal, free, specific and informed indication of the data subject's wishes.
evidence_summary: Section 2 of the Kenya Data Protection Act 2019 provides a statutory definition of consent requiring express, unequivocal, free, specific and informed indication of the data subject's wishes by statement or clear affirmative action.
source_excerpt: "consent" means any manifestation of express, unequivocal, free, specific and informed indication of the data subject's wishes by a statement or by a clear affirmative action, signifying agreement to the processing of personal data.
interpretation: The statutory definition imposes a high, consent-opt-in standard: consent must be express and informed, and cannot be inferred from inaction.
citation: Data Protection Act, 2019 (No. 24 of 2019), s.2 (Kenya Gazette Supplement No. 181), s.2.
methodology_or_basis: Direct quote from the primary legal text (section 2, interpretation).

title: Kenya DPA grants data subjects enumerated rights
claim: The Kenya Data Protection Act, 2019 grants data subjects rights to be informed, to access, to object, to correction and to deletion of personal data.
evidence_summary: Section 26 of the Kenya Data Protection Act 2019 enumerates data subject rights including information, access, objection, correction and deletion of personal data.
source_excerpt: 26. A data subject has a right — (a) to be informed of the use to which their personal data is to be put; (b) to access their personal data in custody of data controller or data processor; (c) to object to the processing of all or part of their personal data; (d) to correction of false or misleading data; and (e) to deletion of false or misleading data about them.
interpretation: The Act codifies individual data-subject rights enforceable against controllers, indicating a rights-based approach to data governance.
methodology_or_basis: Direct quote from the primary legal text (section 26).

title: Kenya DPA: establishment of the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner
claim: The Kenya Data Protection Act, 2019 establishes the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner as a body corporate with its own legal personality, powers and functions.
evidence_summary: Section 5 of the Kenya Data Protection Act 2019 establishes the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner as a body corporate with perpetual succession, capable of suing and being sued, contracting and performing legal acts necessary for its functions.
source_excerpt: There is established the office of the Data Protection Commissioner which shall be a body corporate with perpetual succession and a common seal and shall in its corporate name, be capable of — (a) suing and being sued; (b) taking, purchasing or otherwise acquiring, holding, charging or disposing of movable and immovable property; (c) entering into contracts; and (d) doing such other legal acts necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the [Office].
interpretation: Normative/institutional evidence that Kenya has a dedicated statutory data protection regulator with independent legal personality. Establishes institutional design; does not evidence regulatory effectiveness.
methodology_or_basis: Direct quote from the primary legal text (section 5).

title: Kenya DPA: cross-border transfers permitted only with safeguards
claim: The Kenya Data Protection Act, 2019 permits transfer of personal data out of Kenya only where the controller or processor has provided proof to the Data Commissioner of appropriate safeguards for security and protection of the data.
evidence_summary: Section 48 of the Kenya Data Protection Act 2019 (Part VI, Transfer of Personal Data Outside Kenya) provides that a data controller or processor may transfer personal data to another country only where proof has been given to the Data Commissioner of appropriate safeguards with respect to security and protection of the personal data.
source_excerpt: 48. A data controller or data processor may transfer personal data to another country only where — (a) the data controller or data processor has given proof to the Data Commissioner on the appropriate safeguards with respect to the security and protection of the personal data.
interpretation: Normative evidence of a conditional (safeguards-based) cross-border transfer regime in Kenya, in contrast to the territorial storage mandate in Ethiopia's PDP 1321/2024. Establishes the legal rule; does not evidence enforcement.
methodology_or_basis: Direct quote from the primary legal text (section 48).
keywords: Kenya, cross-border transfer, data sovereignty, safeguards
